question:
**Fill in the Blank: **

Doctrine of Severability allows the _____ part of a law to be retained.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Valid**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Doctrine of Severability refers to the ability of the judiciary to separate the **valid portions of a law** from the invalid or unconstitutional ones.
 
• It is enshrined in Article 13 of the Indian Constitution, which ensures that any law inconsistent with or violating Fundamental Rights is void to the extent of its inconsistency.
 
• Under this doctrine, only the unconstitutional or invalid parts of a legislation are struck down, while the valid parts remain enforceable.
 
• The doctrine ensures that the entire law is not invalidated but retains the **valid and constitutional provisions**.
 
• This principle is applied to protect the legislative intent and preserve the valid portions of the law wherever possible, ensuring a balance between judicial review and legislative sovereignty.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Repealed:**

 
 
• When a law is repealed, it is formally revoked or annulled, either partially or fully, by legislative authority.
 
• Repealing a law completely removes its legal enforceability and existence.
 
• This is different from severability, where only the unconstitutional parts are struck down, and the rest of the law remains intact.
 
 
 
• **Inconsistent:**
 
 
• The term "inconsistent" refers to provisions in a law that conflict with or violate the Constitution, particularly Fundamental Rights.
 
• As per Article 13 of the Indian Constitution, laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are declared void to the extent of their inconsistency.
 
• However, inconsistent provisions are not retained under the Doctrine of Severability; only valid ones are upheld.
 
 
 
• **Unconstitutional:**
 
 
• Any law, policy, or action that contravenes the provisions of the Constitution is deemed unconstitutional.
 
• Unconstitutional laws are struck down by courts during judicial review. The Doctrine of Severability ensures that only unconstitutional parts of a law are invalidated, preserving the valid portions.
